title: Vibe Coding Foundations: From Idea to Launched
description: The LVAI starting point: turn an idea into a real, launched app by pairing the speed of AI building with architecture-first discipline. No coding experience needed.

lessons.title: What Vibe Coding Really Is
lessons.bodyMd:
## Building software by describing it

Vibe coding is the process of using AI and agent tools to build software simply by prompting. Prompting means typing (or speaking) your natural language thoughts onto a screen and letting the AI turn them into a working product. The concept is simple: you vibe along with your ideas, and the AI does the heavy lifting of writing code.

A few years ago, building an app meant learning a programming language first, which could take a year or more. Today you can describe what you want in plain words, the way you would explain it to a friend, and watch an AI builder create the screens, the buttons, and the logic behind them. That is the vibe.

## Two principles that make it work

There are two principles you need to understand before you touch any tool.

First, AI has absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge, but accessing it is a process. If you do not tell it directly what you want, it might invent details to make things easier. It may tell you something is true even when it is not, because it does not want to do the extra work of finding the correct answer. But if you give it concrete, definite instructions, it can route to a much better answer. Vague wishes produce vague software. Clear directions produce working software.

Second, every piece of software has an architecture. Architecture is the organized structure of parts that make the thing work. A website has a front end (the pages people see), a backend (the code that makes it operate), storage (where files live), a database (the organized information, like a spreadsheet), and sign-in (which separates one user from another). If you do not architecture it correctly, the system may not work, no matter how pretty it looks.

## Why this guide exists

Most vibe coding tutorials show you the fun part, which is generating an app in minutes, and skip the part that decides whether the app survives contact with real users. LVAI exists to teach both. Our promise is one sentence: start with a vibe, build with a foundation. You will move fast with AI, but you will work from a plan, verify the work, and set safe limits. That combination is what turns a demo into a product.

## Your first exercise

Grab a notebook or open a notes app. Write down one idea you would build if building software were easy. Do not filter it. A booking page for your side business, a directory of local tutors, a simple store for your art, anything. Write two or three sentences about what it does and who it is for.

That note is the seed of everything in this guide. By the final chapter, you will know exactly how to turn it into a launched version 1.

## Checklist: you are ready for lesson 2 when

- You can explain vibe coding in one sentence to a friend.
- You know the two principles: direct the AI clearly, and respect the architecture.
- You have written down your one idea.

lessons.title: Why the Door Just Opened for You
lessons.bodyMd:
## The barrier fell, not your standards

For decades, software belonged to people who could code. If you had an idea but could not program, you had three options: learn to code, hire someone expensive, or give up. Most people gave up. That is why so many good ideas never became real products.

AI changed the equation. The coding part, the part that used to take years to learn, can now be done conversationally. What remains, and what still matters enormously, is everything around the code: knowing what to build, who it is for, how the parts fit together, and whether it actually works. Those are thinking skills, not typing skills. You already have the raw material for them.

## What ordinary people are building

People with no technical background are now shipping real things: appointment schedulers for salons, directories of local services, simple online stores, client portals for freelancers, internal tools for small teams. None of these required a computer science degree. They required a clear idea, a simple plan, and the patience to test.

LVAI exists to help one million people do exactly this: create tools, systems, and businesses for their personal and professional lives using AI. Not one million programmers. One million people, period.

## You do not need permission

Nobody is going to certify you as ready. There is no exam before your first build. The tools are waiting, the knowledge is available, and the only real prerequisite is a problem you care about solving. This guide will give you the method. The motivation has to come from your idea.

## Your exercise: the problem list

Write down three small problems in your life or work that software could fix. Examples: tracking inventory for a side business, collecting RSVPs without group-chat chaos, showing your portfolio to clients in one link. Keep each to one sentence.

Circle the one that excites you most. That is your candidate project for the rest of this guide. Everything you learn from here on, you will apply to it, so pick the problem you would most love to see solved in your own daily life.

## Checklist: you are ready for lesson 3 when

- You can name the old barrier (had to code) and the new reality (describe and direct).
- You believe, even a little, that a non-programmer can ship software.
- You have three problems written down and one circled.

lessons.title: Fear Is Normal. Start Anyway.
lessons.bodyMd:
## The intimidation is the point of entry

Here is something the LVAI mission states openly: most people feel fear and intimidation around AI. If you feel it too, you are not behind. You are exactly the person this was built for.

The fear usually sounds like this: everyone else already knows this stuff. I will break something. I am not technical enough. AI will replace whatever I build anyway. Each of these is normal, and each of them dissolves with one small win. You do not need courage for the whole journey. You need courage for the first step.

## What experienced builders know

Every experienced builder you admire started confused. They still get confused, regularly. The difference is they learned that confusion is a signal to slow down and ask a better question, not a signal to quit. Professional developers search for answers constantly. They copy, they test, they break things in safe places. You will do the same, with an AI assistant that never gets tired of your questions.

AI does not judge beginners. It does not sigh when you ask what a database is for the third time. It answers the same question with the same patience at 2 a.m. as at noon. That makes it the most beginner-friendly teacher ever built, if you learn to direct it well. This guide teaches you how.

## Reframe your role

You are not trying to become a programmer. You are becoming a director. A film director does not operate every camera, but the film does not exist without their vision and decisions. You bring the idea, the judgment about what matters, and the final call on whether something is good enough. The AI brings speed. That partnership is the whole game.

## Your exercise: one question

Open any AI chat tool you have access to. Ask it one question about your circled idea, for example: "I want to build a simple booking page for my dog grooming side business. What are the main parts such a page needs?" Read the answer. Notice that nothing broke. Notice that you now know more than you did two minutes ago.

That is the entire method in miniature: ask, read, learn, repeat.

## Checklist: you are ready for lesson 4 when

- You have asked an AI at least one real question about your idea.
- You can name your biggest fear about building, in one sentence.
- You understand your role: director, not programmer.

lessons.title: The LVAI Promise: Start with a Vibe, Build with a Foundation
lessons.bodyMd:
## The sentence that runs this whole academy

Start with a vibe. Build with a foundation.

The vibe is your speed and creativity: describe what you want, generate quickly, iterate fearlessly. The foundation is your discipline: a clear plan, a sound structure, real testing, and safe limits. Either one alone fails. Vibe without foundation gives you a pretty demo that collapses the first time a real user touches it. Foundation without vibe gives you months of planning documents and nothing shipped.

LVAI teaches the combination. Every guide in this library, every lab, every tool review serves that one promise: a person with an idea can ship a working version 1.

## The three rules of the house

Our positioning comes down to three rules you will see repeated everywhere here:

1. Build freely, but work from a plan. Creativity thrives inside a clear target.
2. Use AI quickly, but verify. Speed is a gift only if you check the work.
3. Use agents, but set safe limits. Power needs guardrails.

These are not slogans. Chapters 2 through 5 of this guide turn each rule into skills you can practice today.

## The mantra you will memorize

There is a teaching line at the heart of the LVAI curriculum, and you will hear it until it is automatic:

Your words are the steering wheel. Your documents are the map. Your testing is the seat belt.

Your words steer the AI, so vague words steer badly. Your documents, the plan and the architecture you write down, are the map that keeps everyone (you and the AI) from getting lost. Your testing is the seat belt that protects you when something goes wrong, because something always goes wrong.

## The flywheel you are joining

Learning here follows a loop: Learn, Practice, Ship, Stay sharp. You learn a concept in a guide like this one. You practice it in a hands-on lab. You ship a real version 1. You stay sharp with the newsletter and new tool guides as the landscape changes. Then the loop repeats at a higher level, because your second app will be bigger than your first.

## Your exercise: write your why

In two or three sentences, write why you want to build your circled idea. Who does it help, and what changes for them? Keep it somewhere visible. On the days the AI misunderstands you for the fifth time, this paragraph is what keeps you going.

## Checklist: you are ready for chapter 2 when

- You can recite the three house rules in your own words.
- You know the mantra: words steer, documents map, testing protects.
- You have your why written down.

lessons.title: A Good Vibe Starts with a Clear Target
lessons.bodyMd:
## The most expensive mistake in vibe coding

The most expensive mistake is not a bug. It is building the wrong thing fast. AI makes it possible to generate an entire app in an afternoon, which means it is now possible to waste an afternoon with unprecedented efficiency. Builders who skip thinking end up with a polished product nobody wants, and they cannot figure out why, because the code works fine. The code was never the problem. The target was.

Thinking before you build is not the opposite of speed. It is what makes speed useful. Thirty minutes of clear thinking can save you thirty hours of rebuilding. This chapter gives you a method for those thirty minutes.

## Meet PAL

LVAI teaches a five-step thinking method called PAL. It stands for Purpose, Audience, Limits, Logic, and Proof. You run through it at the start of every project and every major feature, before you ask any AI to build anything.

- Purpose: what is the real goal, and what problem does this solve?
- Audience: who is the first specific person this is for?
- Limits: what is in scope, what is out, and what are the rules?
- Logic: how does it work, step by step, for the user?
- Proof: how will you know it works?

A good vibe starts with a clear target. PAL is how you draw the target.

## Why each step earns its place

Purpose keeps you honest. If you cannot state the problem in one sentence, you do not understand it well enough to build for it yet.

Audience keeps you specific. Building for everyone means building for no one. One real person with a real need beats a vague demographic every time.

Limits keep you shippable. Every idea wants to become ten ideas. Limits decide which three survive into version 1, and the rest go on a Later list instead of sinking the project.

Logic keeps you buildable. A fuzzy idea cannot be built. A step-by-step user journey can be handed to an AI builder and turned into screens.

Proof keeps you truthful. Without a definition of done, everything feels 90 percent finished forever. Proof is how you know you actually shipped.

## Your exercise: commit to your idea

Take the circled idea from chapter 1. Write it at the top of a fresh page titled with the project name. Under it, write one paragraph: what is the problem, who has it, and what would change if your app existed? This page becomes your project brief, and every lesson in this chapter adds to it.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You can list the five PAL steps from memory.
- You understand why skipping thinking is the expensive mistake.
- You have a project brief page started with your idea at the top.

lessons.title: PAL Part 1: Purpose and Audience
lessons.bodyMd:
## Purpose: the one-sentence product promise

Purpose asks: what is the real goal, and what user problem does this solve? Your answer should fit in one sentence, following this formula: this app helps [who] do [what] so that [outcome].

Examples: this app helps busy parents book swim lessons in under a minute so that weekends stop being scheduling chaos. This app helps freelance designers share project updates in one link so that clients stop asking for status emails.

Notice what the formula forces. It forces a who, a what, and a so-that. If your sentence is missing the outcome, you have described a feature, not a purpose. Features are interchangeable. Outcomes are what people pay for, or change their habits for.

Write yours now. If it takes more than one sentence, your purpose is still fuzzy. Ask an AI to help you tighten it: paste your draft and ask, "make this one sentence and name the outcome." Then judge the result yourself. You are the director.

## Audience: the first specific user

Audience asks: who is the first specific person this is for? Not a market. A person. Give them a name, even a made-up one. Where do they spend time online? What frustrates them about the current way of doing this? What would make them try your thing instead?

Example: Maya, 34, runs a home bakery, takes orders through Instagram DMs, loses track of them weekly, and would try anything that puts her orders in one tidy list. That paragraph is worth more than a ten-page market analysis at this stage, because you can design for Maya. You cannot design for "small business owners aged 25 to 45."

Your first version serves one Maya. Later versions can serve thousands. Every successful product started narrow.

## The trap to avoid

Beginners often write the purpose as what the app does technically: "an app with a calendar and notifications." That is a parts list, not a purpose. Always climb one level up to the human outcome. Nobody wants a calendar. They want to stop double-booking clients. Build for the outcome and the features will choose themselves.

## Your exercise: promise plus profile

On your project brief page, add two sections. First, your one-sentence product promise using the formula. Second, a short profile of your first user: name, situation, frustration, and what would make them switch. Aim for five to eight sentences total. Concrete beats clever.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- Your product promise fits in one sentence and names an outcome.
- You have a specific first user with a name and a frustration.
- You can explain why one specific user beats a broad audience.

lessons.title: PAL Part 2: Limits and Logic
lessons.bodyMd:
## Limits: draw the version-1 boundary

Limits ask: what is in scope, what is out, and what are the rules? This is the step beginners resist and veterans never skip. Your idea wants to become everything. Limits decide what it becomes first.

Start with non-goals, the features you are explicitly NOT building in version 1. Write three to five. For a booking page: no payments yet, no mobile app yet, no multi-staff scheduling yet. Each non-goal you name is a week of work you just saved. Move them to a Later list so they are not lost, just postponed.

Then name your rules: budget (how much will you spend on tools per month?), privacy (whose data will you hold, and how will you protect it?), and time (what is your target ship date for version 1?). A realistic version-1 boundary is small enough to finish and big enough to matter.

Remember the coach's rule: prefer a complete small workflow over a large unfinished product. One thing working end to end beats ten things half built.

## Logic: map the journey before the screens

Logic asks: how does it work, step by step, for the user? Before any screens exist, write the user's journey as numbered steps. For the bakery order app: 1) Maya shares her order link on Instagram. 2) A customer picks a pickup date from the dates Maya opened. 3) The customer chooses items and quantities. 4) The customer enters a name and phone number. 5) Maya sees the order in her list, marked for that date. 6) Maya taps complete when it is picked up.

Six steps, no jargon, and suddenly the app is buildable. Each step implies a screen or a piece of logic. Edge cases live here too: what if a date is full? What if the customer enters no phone number? You do not need every answer now, but naming the questions keeps the AI from inventing bad answers later.

## Why limits and logic go together

Limits decide what you will not build. Logic describes what you will. Together they form the contract you hand to the AI builder in chapter 4. The clearer this contract, the less the AI invents, and the fewer surprises you get.

## Your exercise: boundaries plus journey

On your project brief, add your Limits section: three to five non-goals, your budget, your privacy note, and your version-1 ship date. Then add your Logic section: the numbered user journey, five to ten steps, including at least two edge cases. Read it aloud. If a friend could follow it, it is clear enough.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You have three to five explicit non-goals on a Later list.
- Your budget, privacy note, and ship date are written down.
- Your user journey reads as clear numbered steps with edge cases.

lessons.title: PAL Part 3: Proof and Your One-Page PRD
lessons.bodyMd:
## Proof: define done before you start

Proof asks: how will you know it works? For each step of your user journey, write one acceptance check, a plain sentence describing what success looks like. A customer can pick a date and see it confirmed on screen. Maya sees new orders appear in her list within seconds. A full date cannot be overbooked.

These checks become your launch gate: the list your version 1 must pass before you share it with real users. No gate, no launch. This single habit separates builders who ship from builders who tinker forever, because it turns the vague feeling of done into a checklist you can actually complete.

Proof also covers how you will test, which chapter 5 expands into a full test plan. For now, the acceptance checks are enough.

## Your words are the steering wheel

Here is the first line of the LVAI mantra: your words are the steering wheel. Everything you just wrote, the promise, the user, the limits, the journey, the proof, becomes the steering input for the AI. When your words are vague, the AI swerves. When they are concrete, it drives straight.

This is why we did PAL before touching any tool. You now hold the single most valuable asset in vibe coding: a clear, written, one-page description of what to build. Professionals call this a PRD, a Product Requirements Document. Yours is written in plain words, and that is a feature, not a weakness.

## Assemble your one-page PRD

Combine everything onto one page with these headings: Product promise (one sentence), First user (short profile), Version 1 scope (what is in, in bullets), Non-goals (the Later list), User journey (numbered steps), Acceptance checks (your launch gate), Budget and ship date. One page. If it spills onto two, tighten it. Brevity is clarity.

Read it once more and ask: if I handed this to a smart friend who had never heard of my idea, could they build the right thing? If yes, your steering wheel is ready.

## Your exercise: finish the PRD

Complete your one-page PRD today. Then do one brave thing: show it to someone. A friend, a potential user, anyone. Ask them what confuses them. Their confusion is free consulting; every unclear sentence they find is a misunderstanding you just prevented.

## Checklist: you are ready for chapter 3 when

- Every journey step has an acceptance check.
- Your one-page PRD fits on one page and uses the seven headings.
- At least one other human has read it and you noted their questions.

lessons.title: Every App Is an Organized System
lessons.bodyMd:
## Forget the code. See the restaurant.

Here is an analogy that makes architecture click. Think of a restaurant. The dining room is the front end: what guests see and touch. The kitchen is the backend: where the real work happens, out of sight. The order book is the database: the organized record of everything. The pantry is storage: where the ingredients (your files and images) live. The lock on the front door is authentication: it decides who gets in. And the waiter is the API: the messenger carrying requests between the dining room and the kitchen.

Every app you will ever build has these same parts, in some form. A booking page has a dining room (the page), a kitchen (the logic that saves bookings), an order book (the list of bookings), a pantry (maybe uploaded photos), a door lock (your admin login), and waiters (the connections between them). Once you see the pattern, no app feels mysterious.

## The parts, in plain language

Front end: the public pages people visit. The signed-in dashboard, if your app has accounts, is a second dining room for members only.

Backend and API: the code that makes things operate, plus the messengers that connect the parts. You will rarely touch this directly; your AI builder will.

Database: the organized notebook. It remembers users, products, orders, bookings, whatever your app needs to remember. Think of it as a set of spreadsheets that the app can read and write.

Storage: where files live, like images or documents. Similar to a shared drive folder, but managed by the app.

Authentication and authorization: sign-in and sign-up (who are you?) plus permissions (what are you allowed to do?). The door lock and the list of who gets a key.

Payments: only if you charge money. Many version 1 apps skip this entirely.

Versioning, deployment, hosting: how your app gets onto the internet and how you update it without breaking it. Chapter 6 covers this.

## Why this matters before you build

Remember the second principle from lesson 1: every software has an architecture, and if you do not architecture it correctly, the system may not work. When you ask an AI to build without naming the parts, it guesses. Sometimes it guesses wrong, and you get an app that looks finished but forgets everything when you refresh the page, because nobody planned the database.

You do not need to build these parts yourself. You need to know they exist, so you can check that your AI builder included them.

## Your exercise: label your restaurant

On a fresh page, draw six boxes labeled with the parts: front end, backend, database, storage, sign-in, and connections. Under each, write one line describing what it holds for YOUR project. Example under database: remembers bookings with name, phone, date, and status. If a part does not apply to version 1 (often payments), write "not in version 1." This sketch is the beginning of your architecture map.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You can explain each part using the restaurant analogy.
- You have six labeled boxes with one line each for your project.
- You know which parts are not in your version 1.

lessons.title: Pick a Starter Stack Without Drowning
lessons.bodyMd:
## One tool, one job

A stack is the set of tools you use to build and run your app. Beginners drown here because the internet offers fifty options for every job and every option claims to be essential. Here is the rule that cuts through the noise: every tool has one job, and your stack is the smallest set of tools that covers all the jobs.

The jobs, from your restaurant sketch: build the screens, remember the data, put it on the internet, and (optionally) take payments. That is four jobs. You need about four tools, not fourteen.

## Example starter stacks

For most beginners, an AI app builder covers the first job and often the third. Tools like Lovable or v0 generate the screens from your descriptions and can publish a live link. A database tool like Supabase remembers the data and handles sign-in. A hosting platform like Vercel or Netlify puts it on the internet with a real address. If you take payments later, a payments tool joins the stack then, not now.

Notice the pattern: each tool owns exactly one job. The AI builder does not also try to be your database. The database does not also try to host your site. When each tool has one job and one owner (you), problems are easy to trace.

## How to choose without regret

Three filters decide. First, fit for your skill level: if a tool assumes you code, it is the wrong tool for version 1. Second, fit for your budget: many tools have free tiers that cover a version 1 comfortably; know your monthly limit from your PAL limits and stay inside it. Third, fit for your architecture: the tool must cover one of your boxes from the last lesson, no more.

Ignore hype. Ignore what a forum says every serious builder uses. Your stack serves your project, not your reputation.

## The Stack Key Sheet

Write a simple table with three columns: job, tool, why. Example rows: build screens, Lovable, describes-to-app with publishing included; remember data, Supabase, free tier plus built-in sign-in; put it online, Vercel, connects to my project with one click. If you cannot fill the why column in one sentence, you have not chosen, you have guessed. Research until you can.

Ask an AI to compare your two finalists for any job, then make the call yourself. You are the director; the AI is your research assistant.

## Your exercise: fill your sheet

Complete your Stack Key Sheet with a tool for each job your version 1 needs. Four to five rows is normal. Write the monthly cost of each (free counts) and confirm the total fits your PAL budget. If a job has no tool yet, mark it undecided and give yourself a deadline to decide.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- Every job from your architecture sketch has exactly one tool.
- Each row has a one-sentence why.
- The total monthly cost fits your budget, and undecided rows have deadlines.

lessons.title: Draw Your Map Before You Build
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your documents are the map

Second line of the mantra: your documents are the map. Your PRD from chapter 2 says what to build and why. Your architecture sketch says how the parts fit. Together they keep you and the AI from getting lost, because building software involves hundreds of small decisions, and without a map, each decision gets made twice or made wrong.

Professionals write many documents: specifications, system architecture, data models, roadmaps. You need a beginner-sized version of the same idea: one sketch of the parts and one list of the data. That is enough map for a version 1.

## Data basics: what does your app need to remember?

The database is the part beginners misunderstand most, so let us make it concrete. A database is a set of tables, and a table is like a spreadsheet tab. Each table has a name and columns. A bookings table might have columns for customer name, phone, date, service, and status.

For your project, list each thing the app must remember as a table, then list its columns. The bakery app needs a bookings table (name, phone, date, items, status) and maybe an availability table (date, slots left). Two tables, ten columns total, and the data side of your app is fully planned.

Also note who can see and change each table. Customers create bookings but only Maya changes their status. This is the beginning of permissions thinking, and writing it down now prevents painful fixes later.

## Refine your architecture sketch

Return to your six boxes from lesson 1. Add arrows showing how they connect: the front end asks the backend for data, the backend reads the database, sign-in guards the dashboard. Add your tables under the database box. Add your stack tools as labels on the boxes they cover.

You now hold a complete version-1 map: PRD plus architecture sketch plus data list plus stack sheet. Four pages that answer nearly every question an AI builder will ask you.

## Your exercise: the map review

Show your map to your AI assistant and ask: "Here is my plan for a version 1 app. What is missing or risky?" Read its answer critically. It will sometimes spot a genuinely missing piece, like password recovery for your admin login. It will sometimes invent problems that do not apply. Your job is to tell the difference, update the map for the real gaps, and ignore the noise.

## Checklist: you are ready for chapter 4 when

- Your architecture sketch has boxes, arrows, tables, and tool labels.
- Every table has columns and a note on who can see or change it.
- You ran the map past an AI, kept the real gaps, and discarded the noise.

lessons.title: Talk to the Builder: Prompting That Works
lessons.bodyMd:
## Concrete beats clever

Now the fun part: directing the AI to build. The single biggest difference between beginners who get working software and beginners who get a mess is prompt quality. A weak prompt says: "make me a booking app." A strong prompt says: "Build a booking page for a home bakery. Customers pick a date from available dates, choose items and quantities, and enter name and phone. The baker sees all bookings in a list grouped by date and can mark each complete. Use the stack in my plan. Start with the customer-facing page only."

The strong prompt works because it names the audience, the exact steps, the data, the stack, and the boundary. It is your PRD and architecture map compressed into directions. This is your words as the steering wheel, in action.

## Give it context, not just commands

Context engineering is a fancy term for a simple habit: tell the AI everything relevant before asking it to build. Paste your one-page PRD. Paste your user journey. Paste your stack sheet. An AI with your full context makes dramatically better decisions than one working from a single sentence.

Think of it like briefing a talented contractor. You would not say "build me a house" and walk away. You would share the blueprint, the budget, and the must-haves. The AI is your contractor. Brief it.

## Chain your prompts

Chain prompting means using one prompt's output as the next prompt's input to get a better answer. First prompt: "Based on my PRD, list the screens this app needs and what goes on each." Review the list, fix what is wrong. Second prompt: "Now build the first screen from that list, following these constraints." Each step builds on a reviewed foundation instead of one giant leap.

This also keeps you in the director's chair. You approve the plan before the building starts, which is exactly how professionals run AI coding tools.

## Every build prompt needs three parts

Use this structure for every significant build request:

1. The task: what to build, in concrete terms, referencing your PRD.
2. The constraints: stack, style, what NOT to do, what already exists that it must not break.
3. The definition of done: how you will check it worked, borrowed from your acceptance checks.

Example: "Task: build the customer booking form from my PRD section 4. Constraints: use my existing stack, match the simple style of the homepage, do not create a payments page. Done looks like: I can pick a date, choose items, enter my details, and see a confirmation; the booking appears in the test database."

## Your exercise: write your first build prompt

Draft the build prompt for the first slice of your app (chapter 4, lesson 2 explains slicing). Include all three parts. Read it aloud and ask: could a smart stranger build the right thing from this alone? Revise until the answer is yes. Save it; you will use it for real in the next lesson.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You can explain why concrete prompts beat vague ones.
- You know the three parts: task, constraints, definition of done.
- You have a written build prompt for your first slice.

lessons.title: Build in Small Steps
lessons.bodyMd:
## The vertical slice

Do not ask the AI to build your whole app at once. Build in vertical slices: one complete feature, working end to end, before starting the next. A vertical slice cuts through every layer, from the screen the user sees down to the database and back. For the bakery app, slice one is: a customer can submit a booking and Maya can see it in her list. That is it. No styling polish, no extra features, just the core loop working.

Why slices beat big bangs: each slice is testable, so bugs surface while they are small. Each slice is shippable, so you always have something working. And each slice teaches you something that improves the next prompt. Professionals call this keeping the next step small. It is the antidote to the half-finished everything problem.

## Order your slices

List your features, then sort them into build order: the core user journey first, supporting features second, nice-to-haves last (or never). A good first slice is the smallest thing that delivers your product promise. For a directory app, slice one is: visitors can browse listings. Slice two: owners can submit a listing. Slice three: search and filters.

Put the order in writing. When the AI suggests adding three extra features mid-build, your slice list is the polite no.

## One main task at a time

During a build session, give the AI one main task and at most two small follow-ups. After each generation, review what changed before asking for more. This rhythm, prompt, review, test, repeat, is the heartbeat of vibe coding done right. It feels slower than one giant prompt. It is dramatically faster than untangling a giant prompt's mistakes.

Between slices, update your map. Check off what works, note what surprised you, and adjust the next slice's prompt with what you learned. Your documents stay alive; they are not paperwork you file and forget.

## Your exercise: slice your project

Write your slice list: three to five slices in build order, each described in one or two sentences with its own mini definition of done. Circle slice one. Then run your build prompt from the last lesson against your AI builder for that slice only. When it finishes, do not celebrate yet; testing comes in chapter 5. Just confirm the slice exists and roughly works.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- Your features are ordered into three to five vertical slices.
- Slice one is built and basically working.
- You are prompting in small steps and reviewing between generations.

lessons.title: When the AI Gets It Wrong
lessons.bodyMd:
## It will get things wrong. That is normal.

Here is the truth nobody puts in the marketing: the AI will misunderstand you, invent features you did not ask for, and confidently present broken work as finished. This is not a flaw in your idea or your intelligence. It is the nature of the tool, and handling it well is a core vibe coding skill.

Remember the first principle: if you do not direct it concretely, it invents. Most wrong outputs trace back to vague input. The fix usually starts with your prompt, not the AI's character.

## The correction loop

When output is wrong, run this loop:

1. Name exactly what is wrong, in one or two sentences. "The booking form lets customers pick past dates" beats "the form is broken."
2. Point to the source of truth. "My PRD says only future dates with open slots."
3. Ask for the smallest fix. "Change the date picker to block past dates and full dates. Nothing else."
4. Test the fix before moving on.

Small, specific corrections work. Angry, vague ones ("this is all wrong, fix it") tend to produce new mistakes stacked on old ones. Stay clinical. You are debugging a process, not arguing with a person.

## Review before you accept

Never accept generated work you have not looked at. For visual changes, look at the actual screens. For logic changes, test the actual behavior. You do not need to read code line by line, but you must verify behavior, because the AI will sometimes claim something works when it does not.

This is the verify half of "use AI quickly, but verify." Speed in generating, discipline in accepting. If a change is large or confusing, ask the AI to explain what it changed and why, in plain language, before you approve it.

## Know when to restart the slice

Sometimes a slice goes so sideways that fixing takes longer than redoing. That is okay. Because you built in small slices, restarting one slice costs an hour, not a week. Note what went wrong in your prompt (that is valuable learning), tighten the prompt, and rebuild the slice cleanly.

## Your exercise: practice a correction

Find one thing in your slice one that is not quite right. It can be tiny: a label, a color, a missing confirmation message. Run the correction loop on it: name it precisely, cite your PRD, request the smallest fix, test it. Notice how much calmer and faster this feels than starting over.

## Checklist: you are ready for chapter 5 when

- You have run the correction loop at least once successfully.
- You review generated work before accepting it, every time.
- You know the difference between a fixable slice and one worth restarting.

lessons.title: Your Testing Is the Seat Belt
lessons.bodyMd:
## The line that saves your launch

Third line of the mantra: your testing is the seat belt. You would not drive without one, even though you plan to drive carefully. Testing is the same: it protects you when something goes wrong, and something always goes wrong. AI-generated apps have bugs like any software, plus a special category: confident mistakes, where the app looks finished but silently does the wrong thing.

Testing is also how you earn the right to move fast. The builders who test thoroughly are the ones who can iterate fearlessly, because they know their seat belt will catch regressions. Skipping tests does not save time; it borrows time from your future self at terrible interest.

## What testing actually means for you

Forget the image of engineers in lab coats. Your testing means: click through everything, as a real user would, and confirm it behaves the way your PRD says. Can a customer complete a booking? Does Maya see it? What happens with bad input, like a phone number field filled with letters? What happens on a phone screen, not just your laptop?

You are checking three things: the happy path works (normal use succeeds), the sad paths fail gracefully (bad input gets a helpful message, not a crash), and permissions hold (customers cannot see Maya's admin views).

## Test the slice, then the whole

After each vertical slice, test that slice completely before building the next. When all slices are done, test the whole app end to end as your first user would, following your PAL user journey step by step with your acceptance checks as the scorecard. This final pass is your launch gate from chapter 2. Nothing ships until the gate passes.

## Your exercise: the first click-through

Set a timer for twenty minutes. Open your slice one and use it as your first user would, slowly, deliberately trying to break it. Click every button. Submit empty forms. Use a small phone screen. Write down everything surprising, even tiny things. This list is gold: it is your first real QA session, and you just did it with zero special tools.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You can explain the seat belt analogy in your own words.
- You know the three things to check: happy path, sad paths, permissions.
- You have a written list of surprises from your first click-through.

lessons.title: A Simple Test Plan Anyone Can Run
lessons.bodyMd:
## From scribbles to a test plan

Your click-through list was informal testing. Now make it repeatable with a simple test plan: a list of test cases you can run after every change. A test case has four parts: what you do, what you expect, what actually happened, and pass or fail. Example: do: submit the booking form with no phone number. Expect: a friendly message asking for the phone number, and no booking saved. Actually happened: (fill in when you run it). Result: pass or fail.

Write your test cases from your acceptance checks, which you already defined in chapter 2. Each acceptance check becomes one or more test cases. Add sad-path cases: empty fields, wrong formats, double submissions, full dates. Add permission cases: log in as a customer and confirm you cannot reach the admin pages.

## The bug report format

When a test fails, file a bug report the AI can actually act on. Four lines: what I did (exact steps), what I expected, what happened instead, and how serious it is (blocks launch, annoying but workable, cosmetic). Then paste it to your AI builder with the smallest-fix request from chapter 4.

Good bug reports get good fixes. "The list is broken" gets guesses. "Steps: 1) submitted two bookings for the same date, 2) expected both in Maya's list, 3) only the second appears. Serious: blocks launch" gets a fix.

## Retest after every fix

Every fix can break something else. After the AI fixes a bug, rerun the full test plan, not just the one case. This takes ten minutes and catches regressions while they are cheap. Keep a simple log: date, what changed, tests run, result. When your app grows, this log becomes your safety record.

## Ask the AI to help you test

You can ask your AI builder to suggest test cases you missed: "Here is my user journey and acceptance checks. What sad paths and edge cases should I test?" Review its suggestions, keep the realistic ones, and add them to your plan. The AI is good at brainstorming ways things break; you are good at judging which ones matter.

## Your exercise: write five test cases

Write five test cases in the four-part format: three from your acceptance checks, one sad path, one permission check. Run them against your slice one right now and fill in the results honestly. File a proper bug report for anything that fails, and get it fixed before building slice two.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- You have a written test plan with at least five test cases.
- Every failure has a four-line bug report.
- You retest the full plan after each fix and keep a log.

lessons.title: Set Safe Limits on Agents
lessons.bodyMd:
## Power needs guardrails

Third house rule: use agents, but set safe limits. AI agents can now take multi-step actions: editing files, installing tools, even deploying. That power is wonderful and genuinely risky. A misdirected agent can delete work, publish something unfinished, or run up costs. Safe limits mean you stay the director, approving the consequential moves.

## Your agent rules

Write these down and follow them every session:

1. Approval points: the agent may suggest and draft, but you approve anything that publishes, sends messages, spends money, changes permissions, or deletes data. Say this explicitly at the start of agentic sessions.
2. Small steps: one task at a time, review between steps. Never let an agent run a ten-step plan unsupervised.
3. No secrets in chat: never paste passwords, API keys, or payment details into a chat window. Real credentials go in the tool's secure settings or environment variables, never in conversation.
4. Least privilege: give each tool and each user only the access they need. Your customers do not need admin powers. Your AI builder does not need your email password.
5. Cost awareness: know which actions cost money (API calls, deployments, AI usage tiers) and set a monthly cap from your PAL budget. Check usage weekly while building.

## What to do when something goes wrong

If an agent does something unexpected, stop it immediately, assess what changed, and restore from your last known good state. This is why version control matters: the LVAI GitHub guide teaches you to save checkpoints of your work, so you can always roll back. Think of it as the seat belt for your building process itself.

Never let embarrassment stop you from stopping. Every experienced builder has halted a runaway process. Caution is professionalism.

## Teach others your limits

If you ever invite collaborators, share your agent rules with them on day one. Teams break things when everyone assumes different rules. Five written rules prevent most disasters.

## Your exercise: write your rules card

Copy the five rules above onto a card, physical or digital, and tailor the details to your stack (where your secrets live, what your monthly cap is). Keep it visible during build sessions. Before your next agentic session, read it aloud. It takes thirty seconds and prevents the mistakes you most want to avoid.

## Checklist: you are ready for chapter 6 when

- Your five agent rules are written and customized to your stack.
- You know where your secrets live (secure settings, never chat).
- You have a monthly cost cap and a weekly check habit.

lessons.title: Deploy: Put Your App on the Internet
lessons.bodyMd:
## What deploying actually means

Deploying means putting your app on the internet at a real address where other people can use it. Until you deploy, your app lives only on your screen. After you deploy, it has a link you can share, and that changes everything: real users, real feedback, real momentum.

Modern tools made this dramatically easier than it used to be. Many AI builders publish with one click. Hosting platforms connect to your project and give you a live link plus preview links for testing changes before they go public. You do not need to understand servers. You need to follow your platform's deploy checklist and verify the live app works.

## The safe deploy checklist

Before you ship version 1, run this list:

1. Your launch gate passes: every acceptance check from chapter 2 is green on the final build.
2. You tested the live link, not just your draft: open the deployed address on your phone and a computer, and run the core journey once more.
3. Secrets are secure: no passwords or keys visible in the app or its public files.
4. You know how to update: learn your platform's update flow now (usually: make changes, preview, publish), so your first fix is not a scramble.
5. You know how to roll back: confirm you can revert to the previous working version if an update breaks something. Your GitHub checkpoints from the GitHub guide are your safety net here.
6. Someone else tried it: at least one person who is not you completed the core journey on the live link.

## Deploy early, deploy small

You do not need every slice finished to deploy. Many builders deploy slice one to a private link just to prove the pipeline works, then keep adding slices to the live app. This habit removes the fear of deployment day, because there is no deployment day, just a steady rhythm of small releases.

## Your exercise: ship the link

Deploy your current progress today, even if it is only slice one on a private or unlisted link. Run the six-item checklist. Write down the live address in your project brief. You have now done the thing most idea-havers never do: put software on the internet.

## Checklist: you are ready for the next lesson when

- Your app has a live address you can open on your phone.
- All six checklist items are done.
- You know how to update and roll back on your platform.

lessons.title: Share It and Learn from Real Users
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your first users are waiting

Software improves through contact with real users, not through more solitary polishing. Your launch does not need to be a big event. It needs to be a small, deliberate loop: share with a few of the right people, watch what happens, listen to what they say, and decide what changes.

Start with your first user profile from chapter 2. Share the link with three to five people who match it. Give them one job: try the core journey and tell you what confused them. Confusion is the most valuable feedback in the world, because every confused user represents ten silent ones who just left.

## How to collect feedback that helps

Ask three questions: what were you trying to do, what happened, and what confused or delighted you? Write down their exact words before you interpret them. There is a discipline to this: separate quotes from interpretations. "I could not find where to pick a date" is a quote and a fact. "The design is bad" is an interpretation that could mean ten different things. Fix facts, investigate interpretations.

Thank every tester, even when the feedback stings. People who tell you what is broken are doing free quality assurance for you. The kindest response to criticism is a fix in the next version.

## Turn feedback into decisions

After each round of feedback, sort what you heard into three piles: fix now (blocks the core journey), fix soon (annoying but workable), and later (ideas for future versions). Update your Later list from chapter 2 with the third pile. Then build the first pile as your next vertical slice, test it with your test plan, and deploy again.

This is the improve loop, and it never really ends. Version 1 becomes version 1.1, then 1.2, each one shaped by real use instead of guesses.

## Your exercise: the three-person launch

Share your live link with three people today, along with the three feedback questions. Give them a deadline (tomorrow is fine). When their answers arrive, write down the quotes, sort them into the three piles, and pick your next slice. You have now run a complete product loop: idea, plan, build, test, ship, learn.

## Checklist: you are ready for the final lesson when

- Three to five real people have tried your live link.
- You collected quotes with the three questions and separated them from interpretations.
- Your feedback is sorted into now, soon, and later, and your next slice is chosen.

lessons.title: The Flywheel: Learn, Practice, Ship, Stay Sharp
lessons.bodyMd:
## Look how far the loop has carried you

Think back to lesson 1. You had an idea in a notebook and a feeling that building software was for other people. Now you have a method: PAL to think, architecture to plan, prompting to build, testing to verify, safe limits to protect, and deployment to ship. You have run the full loop once. That loop is the entire LVAI philosophy in motion: learn it, practice it, ship it, stay sharp.

Every app you build from here repeats the loop at a higher level. Your second project will be more ambitious because your foundation is stronger. That compounding is the real promise of this academy, not any single tool.

## Keep the mantra with you

Your words are the steering wheel. Your documents are the map. Your testing is the seat belt. Tape it where you build. Every time a project feels chaotic, one of those three has slipped. Vague instructions? Tighten the words. Lost in decisions? Update the map. Afraid to change anything? Strengthen the testing. The mantra is a diagnostic tool for the rest of your building life.

## Where to go next in the LVAI library

This guide taught you the method. The rest of the library teaches you the tools and deepens the skills. Here is your recommended path:

Start with the tool guides for AI builders: the Claude Code guide teaches you to direct a professional-grade coding assistant, and the Cursor guide covers the AI code editor workflow. Pair either with the GitHub guide, which teaches version control, checkpoints, and safe collaboration: the safety net every builder needs.

When you are ready to connect your app to the world, the automation guides show you how: the Make guide and the n8n guide teach you to automate workflows like outreach, content, and notifications without writing glue code by hand.

Then stay sharp. The LVAI newsletter keeps you current with what is changing in AI building, so your skills compound instead of going stale. New tool guides land regularly as the landscape evolves.

Suggested order: pick one builder tool guide and build your next slice with it, then take the GitHub guide before your project grows, then add one automation guide when you feel the need for it. Learn, practice, ship, stay sharp, on repeat.

## Your final exercise: declare version 1

Return to your project brief. Check your launch gate one more time. If it passes, write the date next to the words version 1 shipped. Share the link somewhere public: a post, a community, a message to someone who needs it. You earned the moment.

Then write your next loop on a fresh page: what did you learn, what will you practice, what will you ship next, and how will you stay sharp? That page is your personal curriculum now. You know how to direct it.

## Checklist: you finished this guide when

- Your launch gate passes and your version 1 has a ship date.
- You shared your app with at least one person beyond your testers.
- You know your next three steps in the LVAI library and your next loop is written down.

Welcome to the one million. Start with a vibe. Build with a foundation.
